title: KARMA SAYS YOU WILL GET WHAT YOU DESERVE. JESUS SAYS SOMETHING THAT COULD CHANGE YOUR ETERNITY.
paragraphs: KARMA SAYS YOU WILL GET WHAT YOU DESERVE. JESUS SAYS SOMETHING THAT COULD CHANGE YOUR ETERNITY.

You have heard people say, “What goes around comes around.” But what if that familiar saying has quietly distorted the way you understand God's justice, your suffering, other people's failures, and the grace that saved your own soul? The difference between karma and biblical sowing and reaping is not a small theological detail. It leads us straight to the cross, where the sinless Savior suffered what He did not deserve so that guilty sinners could receive the mercy they could never earn.
There is something frighteningly satisfying about watching someone who hurt you finally experience pain.
You may never admit it out loud.

But somewhere deep inside, when the person who betrayed you loses the relationship they thought would last forever, when the person who humiliated you is publicly embarrassed, when the person who lied about you suddenly finds nobody believing them anymore, something whispers inside your heart.
“That's karma.”
And for a moment, it feels good.
Almost like justice.
Almost like heaven finally noticed what they did to you.
But there is a question most people never stop long enough to ask.
What happens when the person who deserves judgment is you?
What happens when the secrets being exposed are yours?
When the lies being remembered are yours?
When the broken promises, hidden compromises, unholy thoughts, selfish decisions, and wounds inflicted on other people are traced back to your own hands?
Do you still want everyone to receive exactly what they deserve?
Or do you suddenly find yourself desperate for something greater than consequences?
Something called mercy.
Stay with me, because what Scripture reveals about sowing, reaping, justice, and grace may confront the way you have been looking at your enemies.
And it may completely change the way you look at yourself.
The Bible does teach that our choices have consequences.
But the Bible does not teach karma.
And confusing the two can quietly turn the Christian life into a system of spiritual transactions instead of a relationship with the living God.
In Galatians 6:7, the apostle Paul writes:
The original Greek makes the agricultural imagery unmistakable:
ὃ γὰρ ἐὰν σπείρῃ ἄνθρωπος, τοῦτο καὶ θερίσει.
Ho gar ean speirē anthrōpos, touto kai therisei.
Literally, the sense is: “For whatever a person sows, this also he will reap.”
The Greek verb σπείρῃ (speirē) refers to sowing, while θερίσει (therisei) refers to reaping or harvesting.
Paul is not introducing an impersonal cosmic mechanism that automatically pays people back.
He is teaching moral accountability before the personal, holy, living God.
And the context matters.
In Galatians 6:8, Paul continues:
“For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.” (KJV)
Notice where Paul directs our attention.
Not toward calculating how soon our enemies will suffer.
Not toward celebrating another person's downfall.
Not toward believing that every painful experience must be repayment for a previous wrong.
He directs our attention toward the flesh and the Spirit.
Toward the direction of our lives.
Toward what we cultivate in the heart.
Toward the eternal significance of living in rebellion against God or walking by His Spirit.
And immediately afterward, Paul tells believers not to grow weary in doing good (Galatians 6:9) and to do good to all people, especially the household of faith (Galatians 6:10).
That is a radically different message from the revenge-centered way people often use the word karma.

Karma, as understood in major Indian religious traditions, concerns the moral consequences of intentional actions, often understood within a larger framework of rebirth or continued existence. Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain understandings differ significantly, and none should be reduced simply to the popular phrase “what goes around comes around.”
Biblical sowing and reaping, however, belongs to a different theological framework.
There is one sovereign Creator.
There is moral responsibility.
There is divine judgment.
There is repentance.
There is forgiveness.
There is resurrection.
And at the center of everything stands Jesus Christ.
Christianity does not teach that the universe is an impersonal moral accountant.
It teaches that the Lord is righteous, merciful, patient, and just.
And this distinction becomes painfully important when suffering enters your life.
Because imagine sitting beside a hospital bed, holding the hand of someone you love, watching their strength disappear.
Imagine a mother burying her child.
Imagine a faithful believer losing everything in a disaster.
Imagine a young woman who has prayed, obeyed, served, forgiven, and still finds herself abandoned by someone who promised never to leave.
Now imagine somebody looking at that suffering and saying:
“You must have done something to deserve this.”
Can you feel how cruel that sounds?
Yet when we turn sowing and reaping into a rigid formula, we can end up treating suffering people exactly that way.
We assume blessing always proves righteousness.
We assume suffering always exposes hidden sin.
We assume the successful must have sown well, and the broken must have sown badly.
But Jesus confronted this way of thinking.
In John 9, the disciples encountered a man who had been blind from birth.
They asked Jesus:
“Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?” (John 9:2, KJV)
They were looking for someone to blame.
They assumed the suffering had to be explained by a particular person's sin.
But Jesus answered:
“Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him.” (John 9:3, KJV)
Jesus was not claiming that the man and his parents were sinless.
He was rejecting the assumption that this man's blindness resulted from the particular sins the disciples were trying to identify.
His suffering was not permission for others to pronounce him guilty.
And that should make us careful.
Very careful.
Because sometimes the person you think God is punishing is the very person God is about to meet with extraordinary compassion.
Sometimes the one you are judging is carrying a burden you know nothing about.
Sometimes what looks like a ruined life is the setting in which Christ is about to reveal His glory.
Remember Job.
A man described as upright, who feared God and turned away from evil.
Yet he lost his possessions, his children, and his health.
His friends were convinced that his suffering must reveal some hidden wickedness.
They defended a simple formula: good people prosper, bad people suffer.
But the book of Job exposes the inadequacy of that formula.
God eventually rebuked Job's friends for failing to speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7).
Their confident explanations did not make them wise.
Their certainty did not make them compassionate.
And their religious language did not make their accusations true.
There is a warning here for every Christian who has ever looked at someone else's pain and immediately called it divine punishment.
Not every wound is a harvest of personal wrongdoing.
Some suffering comes from living in a fallen world.
Some comes from the sinful actions of others.
Some comes through persecution for righteousness.
Some remains mysterious to us.
And sometimes, even when sin has contributed to suffering, we do not possess the knowledge to pronounce God's exact purpose in another person's circumstances.
Jesus Himself warned against assuming that people who suffer tragedy are worse sinners than those who escape it (Luke 13:1–5).
Instead, He turned the conversation toward a truth that concerned everyone.
Repentance.
Not because every tragedy proves exceptional guilt.
But because every human being needs to be reconciled to God.
And this brings us to something even more uncomfortable.
You may have spent years waiting for someone else to reap what they sowed.
But have you ever considered what you have been sowing while you wait?
The resentment you keep feeding.
The conversations where you quietly destroy another person's reputation.
The bitterness you have begun calling discernment.
The pride you disguise as spiritual maturity.
The refusal to forgive that you justify because your pain was real.
Your pain may indeed be real.
What happened to you may have been deeply wrong.
Forgiveness does not require pretending otherwise.
It does not mean abandoning wisdom, removing necessary boundaries, or allowing an abusive person continued access to your life.
But Scripture still calls us to guard our hearts.
Because bitterness can grow even in the soil of genuine injustice.
And if we are not careful, the person who wounded us will continue shaping the person we are becoming.
That is why Romans 12:19 says:
“Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.” (KJV)
The Greek expression behind “vengeance is mine” is:
ἐμοὶ ἐκδίκησις
Emoi ekdikēsis.
“Vengeance belongs to Me.”
This does not mean injustice is unimportant.
It means ultimate judgment belongs to God, not to our private desire for revenge.
And immediately after this instruction, Paul tells believers to feed a hungry enemy and give drink to a thirsty one (Romans 12:20).
Then he writes:
Do you see how different this is?
The world says, “Wait until they get what is coming to them.”
Jesus calls us to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us (Matthew 5:44).
The world tells us to enjoy another person's downfall.
Proverbs 24:17 warns us not to rejoice when our enemy falls.
The world says, “Make them suffer the way they made you suffer.”
The Gospel says, “Leave final judgment with God, pursue what is right, and refuse to let evil conquer your heart.”
And that does not come naturally.
Sometimes it feels impossible.
Especially when the betrayal was personal.
Especially when the apology never came.
Especially when the person who damaged your life appears to be sleeping peacefully while you are still trying to recover.
But hear this carefully.
God's patience with a sinner is not proof that God approves of their sin.
Romans 2:4 teaches that God's goodness, forbearance, and longsuffering are meant to lead people toward repentance.
The Lord's patience is not moral indifference.
And delayed judgment is not the absence of judgment.
The apostle Peter explains that God's patience is connected to His merciful desire for repentance (2 Peter 3:9).
That means the person you desperately want God to destroy may still be someone God is calling to repent.
Someone Christ commands you to pray for.
Someone whose salvation would glorify Jesus far more than their humiliation ever could.
And perhaps that is where this message becomes hardest to accept.
Because we often want grace for ourselves.
But consequences for everyone who hurt us.
We want God to remember our tears.
But forget our sins.
We want our failures understood in context.
But our enemies judged by their worst moments.
We want mercy when we stand before God.
And immediate punishment when someone stands against us.
Yet Jesus tells a story that exposes this contradiction.
In Matthew 18:21–35, a servant owed his master an enormous debt that he could not repay.
When judgment approached, he pleaded for patience.
And the master, moved with compassion, forgave the debt.
Imagine the relief.
Imagine walking away knowing that the burden that threatened to destroy your future had been lifted.
But then that same servant found a fellow servant who owed him a much smaller amount.
He seized him.
Demanded payment.
And refused to show the mercy he had just received.
The parable ends with a severe warning about refusing forgiveness from the heart.
Jesus was not teaching that wrongdoing does not matter.
He was exposing the spiritual contradiction of receiving mercy while refusing to extend it.
And now the question moves from the page into our own lives.
Who are you still holding by the throat in your heart?
Whose name still awakens your anger?
Whose downfall have you secretly imagined?
Whose repentance would disappoint you because you would rather see them punished?
Those questions are not easy.
They were never meant to be.
Because the Gospel does not merely comfort the wounded parts of us.
It also confronts the sinful parts of us.
And no one understood the scandal of undeserved mercy more dramatically than the apostle Paul.
Before he became a preacher of Christ, he persecuted the church.
Acts 8 describes his involvement in the persecution of believers, and Acts 9 records his journey toward Damascus with authority to arrest followers of Jesus.
Paul was not simply someone who had made a few regrettable decisions.
He had actively opposed the people of God.
He had caused real suffering.
There were families who had reason to fear him.
Believers who knew his name not as a source of encouragement, but as a threat.
And then something happened on the road to Damascus.
Jesus confronted him.
“Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?” (Acts 9:4, KJV)
The risen Christ did not pretend Paul's evil was harmless.
He exposed it.
He stopped him.
He humbled him.
And then, astonishingly, He called him.
The persecutor became a preacher.
The enemy of the church became a servant of the Gospel.
The man who had sought to silence the name of Jesus began suffering to proclaim that very name.
That is not a story of sin having no consequences.
Paul's conversion did not erase the pain his persecution had caused, and his ministry included immense hardship.
It is a story of grace transforming a guilty man into a witness for Christ.
Paul later wrote:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” (1 Timothy 1:15, KJV)
And he explained that mercy had been shown to him so that Jesus Christ might display His longsuffering as an example to those who would believe in Him for everlasting life (1 Timothy 1:16).
Think about that.
Someone could have looked at Saul and said:
“I hope he gets exactly what he deserves.”
But Jesus had a redemptive purpose that no one watching Saul's earlier life could have predicted.
This is why Christians must be careful about turning another person's past into their permanent identity.
We should never minimize evil.
We should never silence victims.
We should never confuse a claim of repentance with proof of lasting change.
Real repentance bears fruit, and trust may need to be rebuilt slowly.
But we must also never speak as though the grace of Jesus Christ is too weak to transform a sinner.
Because if that were true, what hope would any of us have?
And now we arrive at the heart of the entire matter.
The cross.
The place where every shallow slogan about people getting what they deserve collapses beneath the weight of divine holiness and divine mercy.
Jesus Christ was sinless.
He never deceived anyone.
Never betrayed the Father.
Never committed injustice.
Never harbored wickedness.
Never needed repentance.
Yet He was rejected, falsely accused, mocked, scourged, and crucified.
If earthly suffering always revealed personal wrongdoing, how would we explain Calvary?
The most righteous man who ever lived endured the most profound injustice.
And He did so willingly, in obedience to the Father, for the salvation of sinners.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.” (KJV)
In the Hebrew text, the phrase translated “for our transgressions” is:
מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ
Mippeshaʿenu.
It conveys the sense of “because of our transgressions” or “on account of our rebellions.”
And the phrase:
מֵעֲוֹנֹתֵינוּ
Meʿavonotenu.
Means “because of our iniquities” or “on account of our guilt.”
The passage identifies the suffering Servant's affliction in relation to the sins of others.
Christians understand this prophecy in light of the suffering and saving work of Jesus Christ, as reflected in 1 Peter 2:24–25.
Jesus was not suffering for sins He had committed.
He was bearing the sins of His people.
And Scripture says something astonishing in 2 Corinthians 5:21:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” (KJV)
Christ did not become morally sinful.
He remained the spotless Savior.
But in His sacrificial work, He bore our sin so that those united to Him by faith might receive righteousness before God.
This is not karma.
This is the Gospel.
The guilty cannot save themselves by balancing good actions against bad ones.
And the innocent Son of God was not trapped in an impersonal cycle of moral repayment.
He willingly gave Himself as the sacrifice for sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again, just as the Scriptures proclaimed (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Justice was not dismissed as meaningless.
Sin was not called harmless.
Grace did not arrive because God suddenly stopped caring about holiness.
At the cross, God demonstrated His righteousness while providing justification for sinners who believe in Jesus (Romans 3:25–26).
And that is why the cross is both terrifying and beautiful.
Terrifying, because our sin is far more serious than we like to admit.
Beautiful, because God's mercy is far greater than we could ever deserve.
The Christian hope is not that every wrong action will be offset by enough good behavior.
Our hope is Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
And here is something you need to hear if you have spent years punishing yourself for the person you used to be.
Repentance is necessary.
Confession matters.
Restitution, where possible and appropriate, matters.
Accountability matters.
Consequences may remain.
A marriage may need years of rebuilding.
A reputation may not recover quickly.
A criminal act may still require legal punishment.
A broken relationship may never return to what it once was.
Grace does not magically erase every earthly consequence of sin.
But for those who belong to Jesus Christ, condemnation does not have the final word.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV)
In the Greek, the expression οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα (ouden ara nyn katakrima) carries the force of “there is therefore now no condemnation.”
The word κατάκριμα (katakrima) refers to condemnation or the adverse judicial sentence.
Paul is speaking of the saving standing of those who are in Christ Jesus.
He is not promising that Christians will never experience discipline, suffering, or earthly consequences.
He is declaring something infinitely greater.
Those who are in Christ are no longer under the final condemnation their sins deserve.
Do you understand what that means?
Your past may explain some of your scars.
But it does not have the authority to overrule the saving work of Jesus.
Your mistakes may have consequences.
But they do not have to remain your identity.
Your failures may be remembered by people.
But forgiveness in Christ is not dependent on their willingness to forget.
And the enemy's accusations do not possess greater authority than God's Word.
If you have repented and placed your faith in Christ, do not keep treating your guilt as though the cross were insufficient.
At the same time, do not mistake the invitation of grace for permission to continue in deliberate sin.
Paul confronted that distortion directly.
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” (Romans 6:1–2, KJV)
Grace does not make holiness unnecessary.
Grace brings us into a new life where holiness becomes the fruit of belonging to Christ.
We are not saved by good works.
We are saved by grace through faith, and created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:8–10).
That order matters.
We do not obey so that Jesus will finally decide to love us.
We obey because His grace has brought us into a new relationship with Him.
We do not give so that God will forgive our sins.
We give because His generosity has transformed our hearts.
We do not sow righteousness to purchase salvation.
We walk by the Spirit because salvation is God's gift in Christ.
And if you miss that distinction, you may spend your entire Christian life trying to earn what Jesus freely gives.
You will become exhausted.
Afraid.
Obsessed with whether you have done enough.
Terrified that every setback means God is angry with you.
And suspicious that every blessing means you must be spiritually superior to someone else.
But that is not the freedom of the Gospel.
That is spiritual bondage wearing religious clothing.
The Bible's teaching about sowing and reaping is serious.
It warns us that what we cultivate matters.
A life surrendered to sinful desires is not harmless.
A pattern of dishonesty damages trust.
Unrepentant cruelty wounds people.
Neglecting prayer, Scripture, fellowship, and obedience can leave us spiritually vulnerable.
And walking by the Spirit bears fruit that reflects His work in us.
But biblical sowing and reaping is not a promise that every obedient believer will become wealthy, healthy, admired, and comfortable.
Nor is it a guarantee that every wicked person will face visible punishment before death.
Psalm 73 wrestles with the prosperity of the wicked.

Ecclesiastes acknowledges that righteous people sometimes experience what seems fitting for the wicked, while wicked people sometimes experience what seems fitting for the righteous (Ecclesiastes 8:14).
Scripture does not hide these painful realities.
It teaches us to look beyond appearances and trust the final justice of God.
And one day, every person will stand accountable before Him.
Hebrews 9:27 reminds us that death is followed by judgment.
Revelation 20:11–15 portrays the final judgment.
Our hope is not that we can manipulate the harvest.
Our hope is that the Judge of all the earth will do what is right, and that salvation is found in His Son.
So perhaps the question is no longer, “When will the people who hurt me get their karma?”
Perhaps the better question is:
“Lord, what are You asking me to surrender while I wait for Your justice?”
Maybe it is the hatred you have carried for years.
Maybe it is the need to see someone humiliated before you can feel peace.
Maybe it is the pride that keeps you from apologizing to the person you wounded.
Maybe it is a secret sin you keep excusing because someone else has done worse.
Maybe it is the fear that God could never forgive what you have done.
Or maybe you are reading this while struggling beneath consequences you genuinely brought upon yourself.
You made the decision.
You crossed the boundary.
You told the lie.
You betrayed the trust.
And now you are living with the aftermath.
You cannot rewind the conversation.
You cannot retrieve the wasted years.
You cannot force someone to trust you again.
And sometimes the most painful sentence in the world is:
“I did this to myself.”
But listen.
Even there, repentance is not pointless.
Even there, prayer is not useless.
Even there, obedience is not too late.
Even there, the invitation of Jesus still matters.
Consider the criminal crucified beside Christ in Luke 23.
He acknowledged his guilt.
He admitted that he and the other criminal were receiving the consequences of their deeds.
He also declared that Jesus had done nothing wrong.
Then he turned to the crucified Savior and said:
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” (Luke 23:42, KJV)
He could not climb down from his cross.
He could not spend the next twenty years repairing his reputation.
He could not produce a lifetime of religious achievements.
He had no opportunity to build an impressive public testimony.
He had only his guilt, his approaching death, and the King beside him.
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” (Luke 23:43, KJV)
Do not misunderstand that moment.
The criminal was not innocent.
His earthly sentence did not disappear.
His suffering did not suddenly stop.
But he received a promise from the Savior.
A promise that his guilt could not earn.
A promise that his past could not purchase.
A promise made possible by the grace of Jesus Christ.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that sin is insignificant.
But that Christ is mighty to save sinners who cannot save themselves.
And perhaps there is someone reading these words who has never truly understood that.
You know how to talk about consequences.
You know how to quote Galatians 6:7.
You know how to warn people that they will reap what they sow.
But you have never personally surrendered to the Lord who died and rose again to save sinners.
You have been watching everyone else's harvest while neglecting the condition of your own soul.
Today, stop hiding behind religious language.
Come honestly before God.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Trust in the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
Ask Him to forgive you, cleanse you, and teach you to walk in obedience.
Not because a particular prayer formula has magical power.
Not because tears can purchase salvation.
But because Jesus Christ is the Savior, and everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved (Romans 10:13).
And if you already belong to Him, perhaps today is the day to stop treating every hardship as proof that God has abandoned you.
Perhaps today is the day to stop interpreting every blessing as evidence that you are better than someone else.
Perhaps today is the day to forgive someone without pretending their actions were acceptable.
Perhaps today is the day to repent of something you have been defending.
Perhaps today is the day to stop asking God to crush your enemy and begin praying that Christ will bring them to genuine repentance.
There is no shame in admitting that this is difficult.
Some wounds take time to heal.
Some acts of forgiveness must be reaffirmed through long seasons of grief.
Some situations require protection, wise counsel, and appropriate accountability.
But none of that places you beyond the reach of God's sustaining grace.
And if this message has touched a place you rarely allow anyone to see, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
Not to impress anyone.
Not to pretend you have everything figured out.
But to take one honest step into the light.
You do not have to disclose private wounds or name the people involved.
Sometimes a few sincere words become the beginning of a conversation that reminds another struggling believer they are not walking alone.
And think about the people in your life who may need to hear this truth.
The friend who cannot forgive themselves.
The brother still consumed by bitterness.
The sister who believes every hardship means God is punishing her.
The young believer who thinks Christianity is nothing more than behaving well enough to earn blessings.
The person who has walked away from church because they were told their suffering proved they lacked faith.
Not as a religious performance, but as a way of making the truth of Scripture accessible to someone who may never ask you directly for help.
There may come a day when the old bitterness returns, when guilt begins speaking loudly again, or when you are tempted to measure God's love by your circumstances.
On that day, return to the Scriptures we have considered.
Let the Word of God, not the slogans of the world, shape your understanding of justice and grace.

And if you believe that Christ-centered teaching should reach more homes, more struggling believers, more families, and more people who have not yet understood the Gospel, I want to invite you to become part of what we are building through Gospel Warrior.
Following Gospel Warrior is a simple way to stay connected to daily Scripture, biblical encouragement, honest conviction, repentance, healing, and discipleship centered on Jesus Christ.

Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, those who have grown spiritually indifferent, and even those who do not yet believe in Jesus to follow along and examine the message of the Gospel.
Those resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible, including to people who may not have the means to purchase Christian books or study materials.
But if the Lord has provided you with the means and you believe this ministry is worth supporting, your partnership can help make its work possible.
Paul wrote in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
That is the spirit in which we extend this invitation.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
But an opportunity for willing partnership in work that seeks to honor Jesus Christ.
These products can serve as everyday reminders of Scripture, opportunities for Gospel conversations, and thoughtful gifts for people you love.
Send a free devotional to a struggling believer.
Pray that the Word of God will reach people who need to hear about repentance, forgiveness, and new life in Christ.
Because the mission is not to build admiration for a page.
It is to direct attention to Jesus.
It is to encourage people to become deeply rooted in the Scriptures, connected to a faithful local church, and increasingly obedient to Christ.
And that brings us back to where we began.
The person who hurt you.
The person whose downfall you wanted to witness.
The person whose name still stirs something painful in your heart.
You may never receive the apology you deserved.
You may never see the justice you hoped to see in this life.
You may never fully understand why God allowed certain things to happen.
But you can entrust judgment to Him.
You can pursue what is right.
You can seek safety where it is needed.
You can refuse to celebrate evil.
And you can ask the Holy Spirit to cultivate in you a heart that increasingly resembles Jesus.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that everyone will receive an immediate earthly repayment for everything they have done.
It is the announcement that God is holy, humanity is sinful, judgment is real, and Jesus Christ has died and risen to save all who turn to Him in faith.
Karma and biblical sowing and reaping are not the same thing.
And neither should be confused with the saving grace of Christ.
At the cross, Jesus did not deny the seriousness of sin.
He confronted it through His sacrifice.
At the empty tomb, He did not merely offer a motivational lesson about second chances.
He conquered death and established the certainty of His victory.
And through the Gospel, He does not merely promise to improve your circumstances.
He calls you to repentance, grants forgiveness, and brings you into new life with Him.
So stop measuring your hope by whether your enemies have suffered enough.
Stop measuring God's love by whether your life has become comfortable enough.
And stop measuring the possibility of redemption by how shameful your past has been.
Look to Jesus.
The One who bore sin though He was sinless.
The One who prayed for His executioners.
The One who welcomed a repentant criminal.
The One who transformed a persecutor into an apostle.
The One who still calls sinners out of darkness into His marvelous light.
And remember this whenever the language of karma begins to sound more satisfying than the message of the cross:

If all you wanted was for everyone to receive what they deserved, you would have no Gospel to celebrate—because the mercy that saved you is the very mercy you must never resent God for offering someone else.
